Dengue Fever: Public Health Awareness Guide
A simple reference for community health awareness (for use by health awareness chatbots and community health workers)
Overview
Dengue fever is an illness spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It is caused by the dengue virus and is common in tropical and sub-tropical parts of the world, including most of India. Both children and adults can get dengue. Many people who get infected have no symptoms at all or only mild symptoms, and most people recover fully within one to two weeks with proper rest and care. In a small number of cases, dengue can become severe and needs urgent hospital treatment. Because there is no specific medicine that cures dengue, the best protection is preventing mosquito bites and stopping mosquitoes from breeding around homes and villages.
Common Symptoms
Dengue usually begins suddenly, about four to seven days after the mosquito bite. Common signs include:
Sudden high fever
Severe headache, often with pain behind the eyes
Muscle, joint, and body pain (sometimes called “break-bone fever”)
Nausea and vomiting
Skin rash, which may appear a few days after the fever starts
Weakness and loss of appetite
Mild bleeding, such as from the gums or nose, in some cases
Most people start feeling better after the fever comes down, usually within a week. However, a few people can develop severe dengue just as the fever is going down, which is why it is important to keep watching for warning signs even after the fever reduces.
Causes
Dengue is caused by the dengue virus, which spreads to people through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. These mosquitoes are most active during the day, especially in the early morning and before sunset. They breed in clean, standing water that collects in and around homes, such as in water storage containers, discarded tyres, flower pots, coolers, tanks, tins, and other containers that hold rainwater. Dengue does not spread directly from one person to another through touch, coughing, or sharing food; it spreads only through mosquito bites. A person can get dengue more than once in their life, and a second infection can sometimes be more severe than the first.
When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs – Act Immediately)
Most dengue cases can be managed at home with rest and fluids, but some warning signs mean the person needs urgent medical attention, ideally at a hospital or health centre. Go to a doctor or hospital immediately if the person has any of the following:
Severe stomach pain or continuous vomiting
Bleeding from the nose, gums, or blood in vomit or stool (black stool)
Difficulty breathing or fast, shallow breathing
Extreme tiredness, restlessness, or confusion
Cold, clammy skin or pale skin
Not passing urine for several hours
Fever that suddenly drops but the person feels worse, not better
Any bleeding under the skin (small red or purple spots)
These warning signs often appear as the fever is coming down, usually three to seven days after symptoms start. Infants, pregnant women, older adults, and people with other health conditions should be watched extra carefully and taken to a doctor early, even for mild symptoms, since they have a higher chance of complications.
Home Care and Prevention
Home care (for mild dengue without warning signs):
Rest as much as possible and avoid heavy physical activity
Drink plenty of fluids – water, oral rehydration solution (ORS), coconut water, or fruit juice – to prevent dehydration
Eat light, easily digestible food
Check body temperature regularly and watch for warning signs
Do not take any medicine without consulting a doctor, since some common painkillers can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue
Use a mosquito net or repellent while resting, so the patient does not spread infection to more mosquitoes, which can then bite others
Prevention (stopping mosquito breeding):
Empty, clean, or cover all containers that can collect water – buckets, drums, coolers, flower pots, and tanks – at least once a week
Remove stagnant water from around the house, including in tyres, broken pots, and construction sites
Keep drains clear and avoid letting water collect in open spaces
Use mosquito nets, screens on windows, and mosquito repellents, especially during the day
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs, particularly for children and during outdoor work
Support community and municipal efforts such as fogging and larvicide spraying, and report breeding sites to local health workers
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, dengue follows a clear seasonal pattern linked to the state's monsoon and post-monsoon periods. Cases typically begin rising with the arrival of the south-west monsoon around June to July and peak during the post-monsoon months of September to November, when heavy rainfall combined with warm, humid weather creates ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. Coastal and urban districts, including areas around Bhubaneswar, Cuttack, Khurda, and Jajpur, along with parts of southern and tribal-dominated districts, have historically reported higher case numbers during these months, though outbreaks can occur across most districts of the state.
Because Odisha experiences heavy monsoon rainfall and frequent waterlogging, extra care is needed to prevent water from collecting in open drains, construction sites, discarded containers, tyres, and low-lying areas after rains. Rural households should regularly check water storage pots, coolers, and any containers used for rainwater harvesting, since these become common breeding grounds once the rains begin. Community-level cleanliness drives, timely desilting of drains, and prompt reporting of fever cases to the nearest health centre or Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) worker can help control local outbreaks. Awareness and early action before and during the monsoon season are especially important in reducing the annual rise in dengue cases seen across the state.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and its National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and published research and news reports on dengue trends in Odisha. It has been written in simple language for general awareness and paraphrased in the writer's own words; it is not a verbatim reproduction of any single source.
Sources referred to:
World Health Organization (WHO) – www.who.int
Pan American Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) – www.paho.org
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India (MoHFW) / National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
National Health Mission (NHM), Government of India
Government of Odisha, Department of Health and Family Welfare
Peer-reviewed studies on dengue epidemiology in Odisha (published via PubMed/PMC, ICMR-Vector Control Research Centre)
News reports on Odisha dengue trends (Deccan Herald and other regional media)
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
